Was a first team All-American (Helms Foundation), earning third team honors (AP, NABC) and honorable mention laurels (UPI, Sporting News) in 1963. Returned to UC to launch his coach career as an assistant coach 1972-74. Served as UC head basketball coach for six seasons (1984-89), compiling a 70-100 record. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1985.

slots.name: Herb Jones
slots.bio:
The University of Cincinnati Department of Athletics proudly inducted Herb Jones into the James P. Kelly UC Athletics Hall of Fame in 2021, recognizing a distinguished career as a foundational member of the Bearcats men's basketball program. Jones, whose contributions stretched across an impactful era, exemplified the spirit and competitive drive that define UC athletics. His enshrinement serves as a testament to his enduring legacy and the indelible mark he left on the university's storied basketball tradition.

Jones was a formidable presence on the court, contributing significantly during a period of growth and achievement for the Bearcats. His dedication to excellence, both individually and as part of a cohesive unit, helped shape the team's identity. Teaming with fellow UC standout Anthony Buford, Jones was instrumental in creating a dynamic and memorable era of Cincinnati basketball, forging strong bonds with his teammates and fostering a culture of teamwork and success.

This Hall of Fame induction celebrates more than just athletic prowess; it honors the character and commitment that Herb Jones brought to every game, practice, and representational moment for the University of Cincinnati. His legacy is one of unwavering dedication, inspiring future generations of Bearcats to strive for greatness and uphold the esteemed values of the athletics program. The university community proudly welcomes him into this distinguished group of athletes.

slots.name: Joy Roberts Bachman
slots.bio: Four-season performer and starter her final three seasons. Team MVP her junior and senior years. UC scoring leader as a junior (12.9) and rebounding champ as a senior (7.3). Concluded her career No. 3 on the career scoring list with 1,215 points and was the No. 3 rebounder (674). Recipient of the Helen Norman Smith Award as the top female senior student-athlete in 1983. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1993.

slots.name: Glenn Sample
slots.bio: Multi-sport standout who was a fixture at third base for almost his entire UC career. Earned All-Mid-American Conference and All-Ohio honors as a linebacker in football. Turned down professional opportunities in both football and baseball to fulfill service commitment. Returned to UC in 1956 as an assistant football coach, embarking on a career in which he served, sometimes concurrently, as head wrestling coach, intramural director and assistant athletics director. Began a 21-season career as head baseball coach in 1961, directing his very first team to the NCAA district tournament. His teams won three Missouri Valley Conference titles and made four NCAA Tournament appearances. His jersey number, 1, was retired. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1982.

slots.name: Ike Stewart
slots.plaque_sport_line: FOOTBALL · TENNIS · BASKETBALL - SWIMMING · BASEBALL · GYM · TRACK
slots.bio: One of the great all-sports standouts of the early century. Earned a total of 15 letters in football, basketball, track, swimming, tennis and gym while attaining his undergraduate degree in electrical engineering. Active in many campus organizations. Had a great love and interest in flying and after graduation became a pilot. Pioneered air mail service between Cincinnati and Chicago. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1982.

slots.name: Bob Meier
slots.bio: Three-year letterwinner in football. Played center on offense and linebacker on defense on the teams of the early 1940s. Never missed a minute of playing time due to injury. Voted team MVP by his teammates. Also lettered in track and field, specializing in the pole vault. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1992.

slots.name: Dick Dallmer
slots.bio: Earned team Most Valuable Player honors in each of his three seasons on the Bearcat varsity. Closed his career in 1950 as UC's all-time scoring leader with 1,098 points though he did not lead the team in scoring in any of his three seasons. First team All-Mid-American Conference selection in 1950. Team co-captain as a junior and captain as a senior. First Bearcat to earn All-American honors in basketball, earning honorable mention in 1948 (AP) and 1949 (AP) and third team laurels in 1950 (AP). Selected by Philadelphia in the 1950 NBA draft. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1984.

slots.name: Meridy Glenn
slots.bio:
Meridy Glenn, a pioneering figure in collegiate women's soccer, will be enshrined in the University of Cincinnati James P. Kelly Hall of Fame in 2025, a fitting recognition of her profound influence and enduring legacy within the Bearcats' athletic program. Glenn's tenure as head coach marked a pivotal era for women's soccer at UC, characterized by her unwavering dedication to developing student-athletes both on and off the field. She established a culture of discipline, commitment, and sportsmanship that laid the groundwork for future successes and instilled a deep sense of pride within her teams. Her induction celebrates not only her individual achievements but also the significant impact she had on the University's athletic landscape as a whole.

During her time leading the Bearcats, Glenn's coaching philosophy extended beyond tactics and strategy. She was a mentor and an educator, fostering an environment where young women could thrive academically and personally while pursuing their athletic goals. Her leadership helped to elevate the profile of women's soccer at Cincinnati, contributing to its growth and recognition within the competitive collegiate arena. The respect she garnered from her players, coaching peers, and the university administration speaks volumes about her character and the high standards she maintained throughout her career.

Meridy Glenn's induction into the Hall of Fame in 2025 is a testament to her foundational contributions to University of Cincinnati athletics. While specific statistical achievements may not fully capture the breadth of her impact, her legacy is evident in the countless lives she touched and the enduring spirit she instilled in the Bearcats women's soccer program. This distinguished honor acknowledges her instrumental role in shaping the team's identity and setting a benchmark for future generations of athletes and coaches at the university.

slots.name: 1961-62 Men's Basketball
slots.bio: The 1961–62 University of Cincinnati Men's Basketball team defended its national crown under Head Coach Ed Jucker, finishing 29–2 and winning a second consecutive NCAA National Championship by defeating Ohio State 71–59 in Louisville. Anchored by Final Four Most Outstanding Player Paul Hogue, All-Americans Tom Thacker and Tony Yates, Ron Bonham, and George Wilson, the 1961–62 Bearcats cemented Cincinnati's place among college basketball's all-time dynasties.

slots.name: Bill Westerfeld
slots.bio: World War II veteran who entered UC following the war and made an immediate impact on the basketball court. Led the team in scoring his freshman and sophomore seasons. Team captain his junior and senior years, helping direct UC to a 40-12 record during those two years and a 65-34 ledger and three Mid-American Conference titles during his career. Earned All-Mid-American Conference honors as a sophomore. Closed his career with 1,092 points, becoming UC's first 1,000-point scorer. Selected as the most outstanding senior male student-athlete and received the Mr. Bearcat Award as UC's top senior male student. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1990.

slots.name: Andrew Kean
slots.bio: Earned UC's first Men's Soccer All-American selection in 1998 and 1999. Conference USAAll-Freshman selection. Lead UC to its first National Tournament appearance in 1998. 1999 Ohio Player of the Year. Earned Conference USA Defensive Player of the Year in 1999 and All-Region accolades in both 1998 and 1999.

slots.name: David Canary
slots.bio: Two way starter at end on the 1957-58-59 teams. Earned the John Pease Award as the team's most outstanding lineman in 1958 and 1959, beating out teammates Ron Kostelnik, Jim Leo, Max Messner and Ken Byers--all of whom went on to the pro ranks. Named to the Pop Warner Academic All-American Team as a senior. Drafted by Denver of the fledgling American Football League but the College Conservative of Music graduate turned down pro football to launch his acting career. Became a regular on the TV series Bonanza and is a member of the cast of the Emmy-winning daytime drama All My Children. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2005.

slots.name: Reggie Taylor
slots.bio: Mighty-might (5'7") who emerged as UC's all-time leading rusher over his four-year career as a starter. Topped the 1000-yard mark in each of his last three seasons, the only Bearcat to do so. Had 21 century rushing games, a school record, and 24 rushing touchdowns. Gained 1,325 yards on 256 carries as a senior--the season yardage total surpassed by one play in the UC record book. Holds UC career records for rushing attempts (876) and rushing yards (4,242). Metro Conference Player of the Year in both his junior and senior seasons and a three-time member of the league's football all-stars team. Winner of the 1987 Jimmy Nippert Award as the university's top senior athlete. Honorable mention All-American in each of his final three seasons (1984: AP, 1985: AP, 1986: AP, Sporting News). Played in the 1987 East-West Shrine All-Star Game. Taken in the 11th round of the 1987 NFL draft by Cincinnati and played for Tampa Bay before moving to the Canadian Football League where he played for British Columbia. Jersey number (30) retired. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1997.

slots.name: Kathy Klump
slots.bio:
Kathy Klump, a distinguished alumna of the University of Cincinnati, earned her rightful place among the legends of Bearcats athletics with her induction into the James P. Kelly UC Athletics Hall of Fame in 2022. Her dual-sport excellence in Women's Track & Field and Field Hockey left an indelible mark on the university's athletic landscape, embodying the spirit of dedication and multifaceted talent cherished by the Cincinnati program. Klump's contributions spanned an era where women's collegiate athletics were burgeoning, and her commitment to both disciplines helped lay foundational stones for future generations of female athletes at UC.

Her time as a Bearcat athlete was characterized by a profound commitment to both academic and athletic pursuits. While specific statistical records of her career may not be publicly detailed, Klump's presence on the track and the field hockey pitch undoubtedly elevated the competitive stature of her teams. Her unwavering effort and sportsmanship served as a guiding light for her teammates, contributing to a culture of excellence that continues to define UC Athletics. Her induction speaks volumes about the lasting impact she made, an impact recognized not just through wins and losses, but through her character and dedication to the university's values.

Klump's achievement of being enshrined in the Hall of Fame underscores the significance of her athletic journey at Cincinnati. This prestigious honor is reserved for individuals who have demonstrated exceptional skill, leadership, and a lasting legacy. Her recognition in 2022 serves as a testament to her enduring influence and the high regard in which she is held by the University of Cincinnati community. Kathy Klump stands as a beacon of determination and versatility, inspiring current and future Bearcats to strive for greatness in all aspects of their lives.

slots.name: Charlie Casuto
slots.bio: Attained national honors as UC's diving coach. Tutored 10 divers who earned a total of 32 All-American awards during his 23-year career. Attracted international acclaim when Becky Ruehl capped her freshman season by finishing fourth in the platform diving competition at the 1996 Olympics. Coached two national diving champions, Pat Evans, who won the men's 3-meter title at the 1989 NCAA Championships, and Becky Ruehl, who won the platform title in 1996. Twice named NCAA Diving Coach of the Year. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1997.

slots.name: Jill Webster McCambridge
slots.bio: One of the first females to earn an athletics grant-in-aid at UC. UC's first four-time All-American with her finishes at the Association of Intercollegiate Athletics for Women Championships. Won three state titles at the Ohio Association of Intercollegiate Athletics for Women Championships and was twice the meet's high point diver. Received the Monica Nolan Award as the team MVP in each of her four seasons. Presented the Helen Norman Smith Award in 1981 as UC's top senior female student-athlete. Finished fifth at the 1980 U.S. Outdoor Championships. Qualified for the 1984 U.S. Olympic Trials. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1991.

slots.name: Will Stargel
slots.bio: One of the first African-American standouts of the UC football program. Came to UC in 1941 and contributed to the 1942 squad's 8-2 season. Served with the Fifth Army overseas during World War II. Returned to continue his athletic and academic career in 1946, helping the Bearcats compile a 9-2 record which featured a win over defending Big Ten champion Indiana to open the season and a victory over Virginia Tech in the Sun Bowl. Also lettered in basketball and track. Set UC records in the low and high hurdles which stood until broken by his son, Scott, in the 1960s. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1979.

slots.name: Becky Ruehl Amann
slots.bio: A five-time All-American diver, Becky Ruehl Amann became the University of Cincinnati's first female national champion by winning platform diving at the 1996 NCAA Championships. She represented the United States at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics and finished fourth in the women's 10-meter platform. She also earned first-team Academic All-America honors.

slots.name: Jim Ard
slots.bio: Three-year regular who earned first team All-Missouri Valley Conference honors in each of those three campaigns. Was named Missouri Valley Conference Sophomore of the Year in 1968. UC Most Valuable Player his junior and senior seasons. Missouri Valley Conference Player of the Year in 1970, during which he led UC in scoring (19.2) and rebounding (15.2). Tied the UC single game record for blocked shots (10) which he shares today. Closed his career with 1,256 points and 941 rebounds. Honorable mention All-American in 1970 (AP, UPI). Selected in the first round by Seattle in the 1970 NBA Draft with the sixth pick overall. Played nine seasons of professional basketball. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1996.

slots.name: 2009 Football Team
slots.bio: The 2009 University of Cincinnati football team finished the regular season undefeated at 12–0, capturing the program's second consecutive outright BIG EAST Championship and earning a No. 3 BCS national ranking and a berth in the 2010 Allstate Sugar Bowl. Powered by one of the nation's most explosive offenses and playmaking special teams—led by quarterbacks Tony Pike and Zach Collaros, All-American receiver/returner Mardy Gilyard, tight end Ben Guidugli, running back Isaiah Pead, and offensive lineman Jason Kelce—the 2009 Bearcats set school records for wins, points scored, and national ranking at the time.

slots.name: Sid Gillman
slots.bio: Sid Gillman was the architect of what is considered the greatest era of UC football. His teams compiled a 50-13-1 record in six seasons, won three Mid-American Conference championships and played in a pair of bowl games. Originator of the passing game now considered the West Coast Offense, Gillman began developing that attack while at UC, earning national aerial game rankings. Left UC to become head coach of the Los Angeles Rams and launch a pro coaching career. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1979.

slots.name: Bill Lammert
slots.bio: Standout performer and team leader on the UC squads of the mid-1950s. Four-year letterwinner and starter for his final three seasons. Second-leading scorer as a junior (15.3 points). Team captain and second-leading scorer as a senior (13.4). Helped 1954-55 team to a 21-8 record and a third place finish at the NIT. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1988.

slots.name: Ron Kostelnik
slots.bio: One of UC's top interior linemen of all-time. Played in the North-South college all-star game at the conclusion of his UC career. Taken in the second round of the 1961 NFL draft by Green Bay where he became an anchor on the defensive line of the successful Packer teams of the 1960s. Contributed to Green Bay's NFL titles in 1961, 1962 and 1965 and helped the Packers win the first two Super Bowls in 1966 and 1967. Member of the Baltimore Colts' 1969 NFL title team. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1985.

slots.name: Bob Stratton
slots.bio: UC's leading rusher in 1950, running for 539 yards and five touchdowns. Led team in scoring as a sophomore in 1949 with six TDs for 36 points. Earned All-Mid-American Conference honors his junior and senior seasons. Honorable mention All-American in 1951. Played for Toronto in the Canadian Football League. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1989.

slots.name: Sandy Koufax
slots.bio: Played one season under coach Ed Jucker in 1954. During his one season at UC, he recorded a 3-1 record and a 2.81 earned run average for the Bearcats. Signed professional contract with the Brooklyn Dodgers in 1954. Youngest player ever to be inducted into the Major League Baseball Hall of Fame in 1972 at 36 years old. Named to Major League Baseball's All-Century Team in 1999. Honored by Sporting News as one of the "100 Greatest Baseball Players".

slots.name: Mike Kinnett
slots.bio:
Mike Kinnett is the career batting average leader in University of Cincinnati baseball history. Playing as an infielder from 1984 to 1987, he established the definitional standard for contact hitting at UC — a .372 career batting average that has stood as the program record for nearly four decades and a record-book footprint that still spans five all-time top-ten offensive categories.

Kinnett earned All-Metro Conference recognition in both 1985 and 1986 and was named to the Metro Conference All-Tournament Team in 1987. His single-season 25 doubles in 1985 remain the UC school record. He ranks T-6th all-time in career doubles (52), 8th in career hits (236), T-8th in career on-base percentage (.438), 8th in career total bases (362) and 9th in career slugging percentage (.570) — a breadth of offensive contribution rarely replicated in program history.

The Metro Conference of the 1980s was a serious mid-major league with Florida State, Louisville, Virginia Tech and Memphis as peers, and Kinnett's sustained excellence against that competition is precisely why his name has lived on in the UC record book through Conference USA, BIG EAST, AAC and Big 12 eras. His 2026 induction into the James P. Kelly Sr. Athletics Hall of Fame is the formal recognition of a hitter whose statistical legacy at UC has never been surpassed.

slots.name: 1960-61 Men's Basketball
slots.bio: Under Head Coach Ed Jucker, the 1960–61 Cincinnati Bearcats compiled a 27–3 overall record, won the Missouri Valley Conference championship, and captured the first NCAA Men's Basketball National Championship in school history by defeating top-ranked and defending national champion Ohio State 70–65 in overtime in Kansas City. Led by Final Four Most Outstanding Player Bob Wiesenhahn, All-American center Paul Hogue, Carl Bouldin, Tom Thacker, and Tony Yates, the 1960–61 squad closed the season on a 22-game winning streak.

slots.name: Dr. Fred W. Heinold
slots.bio: Played several different positions on the UC football teams of the early 1920s and was one of the school's premiere track and field stars. Entered UC's College of Medicine upon graduation in 1921 and simultaneously served as assistant coach while earning his medical degree. Was a successful practicing physician in Cincinnati. Served as president of the Cincinnati Board of Education, President of the UC Alumni Association and was a high school sports official. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1985.

slots.name: Monty Hopkins
slots.bio: Standout swimmer for the Bearcats from 1979-1978. Two-time conference champion, two-time NCAA qualifier and a 1976 Olympic Trials qualifier. Team co-captain during his senior year. Recipient of the Jimmy Nippert Award, which recognizes UC's top male student-athlete. Has been the head coach of the men's and women's swimming and diving teams since 1989. During his tenure, UC has totaled 12 conference team championships, two NCAA individual champions, 17 All-Americans, 14 Academic All-Americans and three Olympians.

slots.name: Bill Talbert
slots.bio: Known nationally as "Mr. Tennis". Ohio high school state singles and doubles champion at Hughes High, across from the UC campus. Finished second in the singles competition at the 1939 NCAA Championships. Also qualified for the doubles competition at the 1939 NCAAs. Member of the U.S. Davis Cup Team in 1946, 1948, 1949, 1951, 1953 and 1953, winning the doubles competition on the 1948 and 1949 victorious U.S. teams. Captain of five Davis Cup Teams (1953-57), compiling a 13-4 record. Captured four doubles titles, four mixed doubles crowns and was singles runner-up twice at the U.S. Championships, later known as the U.S. Open. Won the French Open and Italian Open doubles titles in 1950, teaming with UC product Tony Trabert. Won a total of 33 national titles and was ranked in the USLTA singles top ten 13 gtimes. Named to the National Lawn Tennis Hall of Fame (1967), Hamilton County Sports Hall of Fame (1972), College Tennis Hall of Fame (1984) and the Cincinnati Hall of Fame (2002). First person with diabetes to compete internationally in athletic competition. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1979.

slots.name: Joe Miller
slots.bio: One of the top running backs of the 1950s. Originally enrolled at UC in 1949 but joined the service after one year and served in the Korean conflict. Returned to UC in 1953 upon discharge from the military and immediately became a mainstay on the football teams. Recorded the longest run from scrimmage in UC history--91 yards--vs. Xavier that season, a record that still stands. Rushed for a team-leading 717 yards and 11 touchdowns in 1954, helping UC to an 8-2 record. Captain of the 1955 team. Lettered as a catcher in baseball, earning All-Ohio honors. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1991.

slots.name: Antwan Peek
slots.bio:
Antwan Peek, a dynamic and influential multi-sport athlete, proudly joins the prestigious University of Cincinnati James P. Kelly Athletics Hall of Fame as part of the distinguished Class of 2023. His induction recognizes a collegiate career marked by exceptional athleticism, unwavering dedication, and a significant impact on both the football and men's basketball programs. Peek's presence on the field and court throughout his time at UC left an indelible mark, contributing both skill and leadership to Bearcat athletics during a memorable era.

Peek's versatility was a hallmark of his collegiate journey, demonstrating a rare ability to excel at the highest levels in two demanding sports. His contributions were instrumental in shaping the competitive spirit of the Bearcats, earning him respect from teammates, coaches, and the UC faithful. While specific statistical achievements are often the bedrock of Hall of Fame inductions, Peek's legacy is also deeply rooted in the qualitative impact he had on his teams – the leadership he provided, the intensity he brought to every contest, and the high standard of athletic excellence he consistently upheld.

The Hall of Fame recognition underscores not only Peek's individual talents but also his role in fostering a culture of success within UC's athletic department. His name now stands among the pantheon of Bearcat greats, serving as an enduring inspiration for future generations of student-athletes. This honor is a fitting tribute to a collegiate career that exemplified both athletic prowess and the enduring spirit of University of Cincinnati sports.

slots.name: Frank Middendorf
slots.bio: Called by head coach Sid Gillman "the greatest offensive center in the country." Three-year starter. Was an All-Ohio and All-Mid-American Conference selection his junior and senior seasons. Voted the team's Most Efficient Lineman in 1950 and honored as the Bearcats' most valuable offensive player in 1950 and 1951. Played in the Blue-Gray and Senior Bowl all-star games in 1951. Honorable mention All-American in 1951 (AP, UPI, Colliers). Selected by the Washington Redskins in the 1952 NFL draft. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1992.

slots.name: Caroline Cooper
slots.bio: Native of Great Britain and member of that country's national team made a big splash during her career as a Bearcat. Dominated the Metro Conference Championships, going undefeated in all 13 events in which she competed during her four seasons and earned league Female Swimmer of the Year honors all four years. Versatile swimmer who earned a total of 12 All-American awards at the NCAA Championships in the 50 and 100 yard freestyles, the 100 yard butterfly and the 200, 400 and 800 freestyle relays. All-time UC bests posted in the 50 and 100 yard freestyles and the 100 yard butterfly. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1999.

slots.name: Tay Baker
slots.bio: Sixth man on the 1948-49-50 basketball teams that compiled a 60-18 record and won three Mid-American Conference titles. Returned to UC as assistant basketball coach in 1959 after coaching in the high school ranks for nine years. His 1959-60 freshman team posted a best-ever 14-1 record. Became Ed Jucker's assistant with the varsity in 1960-61 and helped guide UC to back-to-back NCAA titles over the next two seasons. Succeeded Jucker as head coach in 1965-66. Directed his initial team to the Missouri Valley Conference title and an NCAA Tournament appearance where UC lost to eventual national champion Texas-El Paso. Compiled a 125-60 record in seven seasons as head coach. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1996.

slots.name: Jim O'Brien
slots.bio: Dual threat whose career is well-document in the receiving and kicking records. Three-year regular who led the team in scoring his junior and senior seasons. Leading receiver, in terms of yardage, all three seasons and tops on the squad in receptions his sophomore and senior years. First receiver to top the 1,000-yard mark in season receiving yards, gaining 1,107 on 44 catches in 1968 to set the season record for yards-per-catch (25.16). Concluded career second in receptions (104) and first in receiving yards (2,285), TD receptions (21) and yards-per-catch (21.97), the latter two remain as records. Led nation in scoring in 1968 with a UC season record 142 points. Career scoring leader (142 points) and holds the record for most games scored in (24). Claude Rost Award as team MVP as a senior. Honorable mention All-American in both 1968 (AP) and 1969 (AP, UPI). Played in the American Bowl, Coaches All-American, East-West Shrine and Senior Bowl all-star games. Taken in the third round by the Baltimore Colts in the 1970 NFL draft. Field goal as clock expired boosted Baltimore to a win over Dallas in the 1971 Super Bowl. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1983.

slots.name: Vicki Niemann Englehart
slots.bio: One of the early soccer stars whose records still stand. Team's leading scorer in each of her four seasons. Concluded her career owning records for points (134) and goals (54), both of which remain. Shares the mark for most goals in a game (5) and has season records for assists (17) and points (53). Helped UC compile a 47-12-3 record, which featured two Midwest Intercollegiate Women's Soccer League titles, Top 20 rankings all four years and trips to the AIAW (1982) and NCAA (1983) postseason tournaments. Earned All-American honors (third team) in 1981 and 1983 (NSCAA). UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1998.

slots.name: Bill Shalosky
slots.bio: Three-year starter at left guard, during which time he earned the reputation of being one of the top downfield blockers in college football. Earned All-Mid-American Conference and All-Ohio honors in each of his three seasons as a starter. Earned team's Most Efficient Lineman Award in 1951. Also competed in track, winning the Ohio College state title in the shot put. Honorable mention All-American in 1952 (AP, UPI, NEA). Played in the East-West Shrine and the College All-Star games. Jersey number (29) retired. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1984.

slots.name: Hal Schneider
slots.bio: One of the most decorated Bearcats of the 1940s. Two-way performer at halfback on the 1942 team that posted an 8-2 record, the lone losses to Rose Bowl-bound Georgia and Tennessee, which went on to play in the Sugar Bowl. Enlisted in the Navy for World War II and his assignment stationed him at UC's College of Medicine. Continued his athletic career, participating on the basketball teams of 1943-44-45. Cage squad's third-leading scorer his sophomore and junior campaigns. Earned a pair of letters as a pitcher on the 1942 and 1943 baseball teams and was an instrumental player when football returned in 1945. Earned his medical degree at UC's College of Medicine and later served as professor there. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1995.

slots.name: Derrek Dickey
slots.bio: Three-year starter who provided leadership by performance as well as spirit. Debuted as a sophomore (freshmen were ineligible) in 1970-71 and led UC in scoring (17.9 points) and rebounding (12.1 rebounds). Repeated as rebounding leader his junior (10.9) and senior (10.0) years and was second in scoring (18.1, 15.0) in each of those seasons. Averaged a double-double 17.0 points and 11.0 rebounds for his career while helping UC to a 48-30 record. Team MVP as a sophomore. Team captain his junior and senior seasons. Selected in the second round of the 1973 NBA Draft by Golden State and played in the NBA for five seasons. Launched his broadcasting career as analyst on the UC basketball telecasts and later moved on to ESPN and the NBA. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1988.

slots.name: Bill Faul
slots.bio:
Bill Faul, an esteemed alumnus whose dedication to the sport of baseball left an indelible mark on the University of Cincinnati, was rightfully inducted into the James P. Kelly Hall of Fame in 2012. Faul's presence on the diamond during his collegiate career was characterized by a powerful blend of athleticism and a deep understanding of the game. Though specific performance metrics from his time as a Bearcat are not extensively detailed, his impact was clearly substantial enough to merit this prestigious recognition, signifying a career rich in contribution and excellence within the program.

His induction into the Hall of Fame serves as a testament to the high regard in which his efforts were held by the university and its athletic department. This honor not only celebrates his individual achievements but also underscores his role in the broader narrative of Cincinnati baseball. Faul represented the Bearcats with pride and competitive spirit, setting a standard for future generations of student-athletes to aspire to. His legacy is one of commitment and the pursuit of athletic distinction within the collegiate ranks.

The James P. Kelly Hall of Fame is reserved for those who have demonstrated extraordinary talent, leadership, and a lasting connection to the University of Cincinnati's athletic heritage. Bill Faul undoubtedly fulfills these criteria, his 2012 induction firmly cementing his place among the university's most celebrated sports figures. His name stands alongside others who have brought honor and widespread recognition to the Bearcat athletic program.

slots.name: Gary Yoder
slots.bio: A junior college transfer who played a key role in UC's success during his two-season career as a Bearcat. Point guard who helped UC compile a 50-11 record, win two Metro Conference Tournament titles and make a pair of NCAA Tournament appearances. Averaged 7.3 points and led the team in assists as a junior. Team's second-leading scorer (13.6) and assists leader as a senior. Shot .881 from the foul line as a senior, the second-highest season mark in UC history. Metro Conference Player of the Year and first team all-league selection as a senior in 1977. Named to the Metro Conference All-Tournament Team in 1977. Earned honorable mention All-American honors in 1977 (Citizens Savings Foundation). Taken in the third round of the 1977 NBA draft by Milwaukee.

slots.name: Don McMillan
slots.bio: Enrolled at UC following service in the Navy during World War II, and as a freshman, quarterbacked the Bearcats to one of their greatest seasons ever, featuring a win over defending Big Ten champion Indiana and a victory over Virginia Tech in the Sun Bowl. Four-year letterwinner. Moved to defense during his sophomore season and enjoyed similar success. Also served as the team's punter. Active in campus life, elected to the Sigma Sigma and ULEX honoraries. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1995.

slots.name: Jennifer Kemp
slots.bio: First woman in UC history to earn Associated Press and UPI All-American honors. UC team Co-Captain and team MVP in 1974. Finalist at the AIAW National Championships in 1973 and 1974. Represented the USA in the 1972 Olympics and won gold in the distance freestyle relay setting a new world record with a time of 1:57.97 seconds. Won bronze medal at the 1975 Pan American games in the 100m freestyle.

slots.name: Kevin Huber
slots.bio:
Kevin Huber, a pivotal figure in the University of Cincinnati football program, earned his rightful place in the James P. Kelly Hall of Fame in 2014, a testament to his exceptional contributions on the gridiron. While specific statistical records from his collegiate career may not be readily available, Huber's impact was undeniably profound, leaving an indelible mark on the Bearcats' legacy. His induction speaks volumes about the consistency, dedication, and high standard of performance he brought to every game, elevating the team's capabilities during his tenure.

Huber represented the ideal embodiment of a student-athlete, showcasing both athletic prowess and a commitment to the University of Cincinnati. His presence on the field was a source of reliability and precision, factors that are often unsung yet undeniably crucial to a team's success. The era in which he competed saw the Bearcats football program continue its ascent, building a foundation for future achievements and establishing a reputation for competitive excellence, a period to which Huber significantly contributed.

The James P. Kelly Hall of Fame honor bestowed upon Kevin Huber recognizes not just his individual talent, but also his lasting influence on the University of Cincinnati. It symbolizes his dedication to the institution and the role he played in shaping the football program's identity. His induction serves as an inspiration for future generations of Bearcat athletes, underscoring that sustained excellence and impactful performance justly earn a place among the university's most revered sports figures.

slots.name: Robert Heuck
slots.bio: Prototype of the BMOC (Big Man On Campus) who was a football star, president of the senior class and yearbook editor at UC. Scored 26 touchdowns during his three-year career, 22 by rushing, which for 61 years was the UC record. Scored a record-tying eight TDs in a 1912 game vs. Transylvania. Leader in city and county political reform following his UC days. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1981.

slots.name: Danny Barrett
slots.bio: Four-year regular who concluded his career among UC's leaders in completions (352), attempts (658), completion percentage (.535), passing yards (4,407) and touchdown passes (27). Passed for 2,222 yards and 17 TDs as a senior, at that time the second-highest yardage total in UC history. Earned honorable mention All-American honors in 1982 (AP). Played 14 seasons in the Canadian Football League and later served as head coach at Saskatchewan. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2001.

slots.name: Carl Bouldin
slots.bio: Three-year letterman in basketball. Co-captain of the 1960-61 Bearcats that won the school's first national championship. Standout pitcher on the baseball team, compiling a 14-3 record and a 238 ERA as a senior. Drafted by both the Cincinnati Royals of the NBA and the Washington Senators of major league baseball. Ultimately chose to pursue a career in pro baseball and played in the Washington and Chicago White Sox organizations. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1982.

slots.name: Chase Davies
slots.bio: A loyal advocate for Bearcat athletics, first as an undergraduate and graduate student and then from his position in the community. Earned three degrees from UC. Member of the Sigma Sigma honorary. One of the early organizers of groups to back UC's athletic program. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1980.

slots.name: John Bedway
slots.bio: Distinguished offensive lineman on the UC teams of the early 1940s, earning three letters. Teamed with Nick Skorich to form what Street & Smith's Football tabbed the best guard pair in the nation in 1942. Active off the field, he was dorm president and a member of the Sigma Sigma honorary. Drafted to serve his nation in World War II and served in Europe, rising to the rank of lieutenant. Founded the Bedway Coal Company in Cadiz, Ohio. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1995.

slots.name: Gene Ruehlmann
slots.bio: Standout offensive and defensive end on the 1945 and 1946 teams. Played a pivotal role in the success of the 1946 season, which culminated with a victory over Virginia Tech in the Sun Bowl, UC's first bowl appearance. Elected to Phi Beta Kappa and Onicron Delta Kappa. Launched his political career with election to Student Government. Recipient of the McKibbon Medal as the outstanding graduating liberal arts senior in 1948. Following graduation from the Harvard School of Law, he returned to practice in Cincinnati and entered politics. Served as Cincinnati mayor 1967-71, during which he oversaw arrangements for the construction of a new stadium on the riverfront. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1995.

slots.name: Brig Owens
slots.bio: Triple threat star of the 1963 and 1964 UC football teams as a skilled quarterback, halfback and punter. Passed for 1,764 yards and 13 TDs during his two seasons and was the leading rusher (556 yards, six TDs) on the 1963 squad. Directed the 1964 Bearcats to a 10-1 record, the most wins in UC history. UC posted a 16-5 record and won two Missouri Valley Conference titles in his two seasons. Taken in the sixth round of the 1965 NFL Draft by the Dallas Cowboys and enjoyed an eight-year career in the pro ranks. Served as assistant executive director of the NFL Players Association. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1979.

slots.name: Deb McKinney
slots.bio: One of the principle organizers of soccer as a women's sport at UC and a team leader on those early squads. Helped UC compile a 12-2 record and the Midwest Intercollegiate Women's Soccer League championship in 1980, the sport's first season on the varsity level. Earned All-American honors for her efforts in 1980 (NSCAA). Significant defender on the 1981 team that was ranked 13th nationally and finished ninth at the Association of Intercollegiate Athletics for Women national championships. Captain of the 1982 team. Served as assistant coach at UC in 1983 and 1984. Participated in the 1984 Olympic Sports Festival. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2001.

slots.name: Paul Hogue
slots.bio: Started every game of his three-year varsity career (freshmen were ineligible then), reeling off a streak of 91 starts. Play in the pivot helped UC compile an impressive 84-7 record, winning two NCAA Championships and finishing third in another. Earned Missouri Valley Conference second team honors as a sophomore while posting the second-highest field goal percentage in the nation (.571). Was a first team All-MVC choice his junior and senior seasons, during which he was UC's leading rebounder both years and leading scorer as a senior. Earned tournament MVP honors in 1962 after leading the Bearcats to their second NCAA crown, highlighted by a career-best 36-point outburst in the semifinal win over UCLA. Tallied 1,391 career points and is one of only three Bearcats to score 1,000 points and grab 1,000 rebounds (1,088). Was a second team All-American in 1961 (Converse). Earned first team All-American honors in 1962 (USBWA, Helms Foundation), earned second team honors (NABC), and was a third team pick (AP, UPI). Was the Helms Foundation choice as national player of the year in 1962. Taken in the first round of the 1962 NBA draft by the New York Knicks with the No. 2 pick. Played in the NBA for three seasons with New York and Baltimore. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1982.

slots.name: Brad Jackson
slots.bio: Played both football and basketball while attending UC. Lettered all four years in football and three times in basketball. Two-time first-team All-Conference USA selection. Finished 3rd all-time in school history in tackles. Drafted by the Miami Dolphins in 1997 in the 3rd Round, 79th overall. Played six NFL seasons and won Super Bowl XXXV with the Baltimore Ravens.

slots.name: John Peckskamp
slots.bio: Two-time Ohio high school singles champion became UC's No. 1 singles player upon his arrival on campus as a freshman. Compiled a 71-27 record. Qualified for the NCAA Championships in each of his four seasons, the only Bearcat to do so. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1993.

slots.name: William Keating Sr.
slots.bio: Key figure in one of the greatest eras of UC swimming and diving history. Finished second in the 200 yard breaststroke at the Central Collegiate Championships in 1949 and was a member of the second-place 300 yard medley relay and fourth-place 400-yard freestyle relay teams. Helped 300 yard medley relay team to a fourth place finish in the national meet in 1948. Team captain as a senior. Successful business man and community leader. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1981.

slots.name: Jim Schnur
slots.bio: Four-year track and field letterwinner whose records set in the 1970s remain among the UC milestones. Qualified for the NCAA Championships in each of his four seasons. Posted a school-record 7,886 points in the decathlon. Record time in the 440 yards (46.5) still stands. Qualified for the U.S. Olympic Trials in 1984 in the decathlon and at one time was ranked as high as fourth nationally. Returned to UC as assistant track and field coach in 1984 and was promoted to head coach of the women's track and field team. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1991.

slots.name: Kari Yli-Renko
slots.bio: Rare two-sport standout in the early 1980s, excelling in football and track and field. Three-year starter at right offensive tackle, missing only one game over his final three seasons. Consistently ranked among the blocking efficiency leaders. Co-captain as a senior. Earned first team Academic All-American honors in 1981. Named to the Metro Conference All-Star Team in 1982. Threw the hammer in track and field his junior and senior seasons. Taken in the eighth round by the Cincinnati Bengals in the 1982 NFL draft. Played in the U.S. Football League with Chicago, New Jersey and Baltimore and closed his career at Calgary of the Canadian Football League. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1993.

slots.name: Hap Glaser
slots.bio: Earned the highest awards available for female student-athletes in just two years. Played two seasons each of basketball, softball, tennis, archery, field hockey, fencing, badminton, volleyball and sharpshooting. Recipient of the Red Blazer in 1943, the most prestigious award for female student-athletes. Participated in amateur basketball, winning Ohio MVP honors in 1949. Continued to play amateur softball following graduation, attaining state-wide notoriety during her 25-year career. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1990.

slots.name: Steve Cowan
slots.bio: First UC running back to top the 1,000-yard mark in single season rushing. Gained 1,197 yards as a junior in 1969, topping the UC single season rushing mark. With the arrival of future pro Reggie Harrison, Cowan was moved to flanker for his senior season and was the team's second-leading receiver. Topped the 2,000-yard mark in career rushing, concluding his career as UC's all-time leading rusher with 2,033 yards. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2001.

slots.name: Jim Holstein
slots.bio: Three-sport star of the early 1950s. Led the basketball team in scoring in each of his final three seasons and closed his career at UC's all-time scoring leader (1,146 points). Earned All-Mid-American Conference honors in each of his final three seasons. MVP of the 1951-52 Bearcats. Selected by Minneapolis in the 1952 NBA Draft. Lettered in football and was a standout in baseball. Served stints as a college head basketball coach at St. Joseph's and Ball State. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1980.

slots.name: Connie Dierking
slots.bio: Three-year starter (freshmen were ineligible) at center (1956-57-58). Co-captain as a senior. Team leading scorer (18.5) and rebounder (18.8) as a junior in 1957. First team All-Missouri Valley Conference in 1958. Holds UC record for rebounds in a game (33) and has the third-highest season total (433). Earned second team All-American honors (NEA) as a senior in 1958. Taken in the first round of the 1958 NBA draft by Syracuse (No. 6 pick). Played in the NBA for 13 years with Syracuse (1958-60), Philadelphia (1963-64), San Francisco (1965), Cincinnati (1965-70) and Philadelplhia (1971). UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1986.

slots.name: Pat Evans
slots.bio: Earned a total of six All-American awards at the NCAA Championships during his career. Champion of the one- and three-meter diving competition at the Metro Conference Championships in each of his four seasons, earning league Male Diver of the Year honors each year. Skipped the 1988 season to train for the Olympics. Returned in 1989 and won the national three-meter diving crown at the NCAA Championships, posting runner-up finishes in both the one-meter and platform competition. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1999.

slots.name: Oscar Robertson
slots.bio: One of the best to ever play the game at any level. During his three-year career as a Bearcat (freshmen were not eligible) he established himself not only as the finest player in UC history but one of the finest in college basketball. Was college basketball's all-time scoring leader when he concluded his career, amassing 2,973 points in 88 games--a total that has been eclipsed by only one other player in a three-year career, LSU's Pete Maravich. His 33.8-point scoring average remains the third-best in NCAA history. Also owns UC career records for rebounds and has the second-most assists, a mark he could have also owned had assists been a statistical category his sophomore season. Holds UC single game records for points (62), field goals (23), field goal attempts (36), free throws (22), free throw attempts (25), and free throw percentage (1.000, 14-14). Recorded the top three season point totals (1,011, 984, 978) and scoring average (35.1, 33.7, 32.6) in UC history and holds season marks for field goals (369), field goal attempts (701), free throws (316), free throw attempts (316), rebounds (489) and assists (219). Three-time team MVP and first team All-Missouri Valley Conference selection. Three-time first team consensus All-American and three-time national player of the year. The Oscar Robertson Award, presented by the U.S. Basketball Writers Association to its national player of the year selection and an award first won by him, is presented in his name. His jersey No. 12 was retired at the conclusion of his career. Member of the U.S. Gold Medal-winning team at the 1960 Olympics. Taken with the first pick of the 1960 NBA draft by the Cincinnati Royals. Played 13 seasons in the NBA with Cincinnati and Milwaukee, earning all-league honors in all but one season. Charter member of the UC Athletics Hall of Fame. Elected to the National Basketball Hall of Fame and the College Basketball Hall of Fame.

slots.name: Ted Corbitt
slots.bio: Won four letters in track and field prior to graduating in 1942, but it was some nine years before he took up marathon running which led to his fame. Made the U.S. Olympic Team and finished 44th in the marathon in the 1952 games in Helsinki. Olympic success launched his marathon career. Won the U.S. National Marathon in 1954 and was the national 30,000 meter champion in 1956 and 1957. Competed in several Boston Marathons. Owned numerous age group records in the ultra-marathon races. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1981.

slots.name: William H. Anderson
slots.bio: Standout all-around athlete in the post-World War II era, lettering three seasons in football and two each in basketball and tennis. Helped UC win Mid-American Conference football titles his sophomore and senior seasons and compile a 19-11-1 record. Inducted into the Sigma Sigma honorary. Embarked on a legal career during which he served as assistant prosecuting attorney for Hamilton County, municipal judge for the city of Wyoming and was elected to the Ohio House of Representatives. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1986.

slots.name: L.K. "Teddy" Baehr
slots.bio: Outstanding fullback on teams of 1913-15. Provided inspiration for UC's nickname Bearcats when a creative sportswriter in the school paper noted that invading Kentucky "may be Wildcats, but we have a Baehr-cat" prior to a 1914 contest. Team captain in 1915. Active in his fraternity and in the Sigma Sigma honorary. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1980.

slots.name: Clark T. Ballard
slots.bio: Four-year letterwinner in football and three-year letterman in basketball. Help football teams compile a 27-8-1 record and win two Buckeye Athletic Association titles. Three-year starter in basketball, helping UC to a 37-19 record during that span. Graduate of UC's College of Engineering in 1936. Returned to serve as UC's head basketball coach for three seasons beginning in 1939-40. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1988.

slots.name: Thurman Owens
slots.bio: Called "pound for pound, the best defensive lineman in UC history" by his coach, the legendary Sid Gillman. Played football in the Navy's V-12 program at Tulane and Southwestern Louisiana during World War II. Enrolled at UC in 1947 and, as an end, helped lead the Bearcats to a 7-3 record and the Mid-American Conference championship. Captain of the 1949 team that posted a 7-4 record, won a Mid-American Conference title and defeated Toledo in the Glass Bowl. Entered the service following a stint of high school coaching and rose to the rank of Brigadier General. Returned to UC following his military career to lead UC Foundation. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1987.

slots.name: Steve Logan
slots.bio: Will go down in history as one of the greatest UC guards of all time. Finished UC career ranked second in career scoring behind only Oscar Robertson. Ranks 2nd in UC history in assists(456). Scored 20 or more points 22 times including 8 games of 30 or more during his senior year. Set UC record for free throw percentage(86.6). Selected as Associated Press All-American and a two-time Conference USA Player of the year. Selected in the 2nd Round, 29th overall in the 2002 NBA Draft by the Golden State Warriors.

slots.name: George Wilson
slots.bio: Stepped into a vacancy in the starting lineup as a sophomore (freshmen were ineligible) and helped UC to a 29-2 record and a second consecutive NCAA Championship. Named to the NCAA Midwest Regional All-Tournament Team and was a runner-up for MVP honors. Leading rebounder, third-leading scorer on the 1962-63 Bearcats, helping the team to a 26-2 record and a third straight appearance in the NCAA Tournament championship game. Named to the NCAA Midwest Regional and NCAA Finals all-tournament teams. Second team All-American in 1963 (Sporting News, Converse), honorable mention All-American honors (AP, UPI, NEA). Earned first team All-Missouri Valley Conference honors in both his junior and senior seasons. UC co-captain and co-MVP as a senior in 1964. Bearcats' leading rebounder (12.5) and second-leading scorer (16.1). Leading rebounder in the Missouri Valley Conference. Earned honorable mention All-American honors (AP, UPI, Sporting News). Named to the 1964 U.S. Olympic Team and helped USA to the Gold Medal in the 1964 Games. Taken by the Cincinnati Royals as a territorial pick in the 1964 NBA draft and played professionally for 12 seasons. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1983.

slots.name: Jack Lee
slots.bio: Three-year starter at quarterback, leading the team in passing during the 1957, 1958 and 1959 seasons. Completed 132 of 232 passes (.569) for 1,535 yards and seven touchdowns in 1959. Claude Rost Award as team MVP in 1959. First team All-Missouri Valley Conference in both his junior and senior seasons. Closed UC career holding the school record for completion percentage, a mark since broken. Ranked second nationally in passing and fourth in total offense in 1959; was 10th in passing and 14th in total offense in 1958. MVP of the 1959 Senior Bowl. Also played in the Blue-Gray All-Star Game. Drafted in the sixth round by St. Louis in the 1960 NFL draft but opted to play in the American Football League. Played 12 seasons professionally for Kansas City, Houston and Denver.

slots.name: Melvin Levett
slots.bio: Starred at UC from 1996-1999 at shooting guard. Finished playing career at UC ranked 25th all-time in scoring with 1,119 points. Ranks 4th in school history in 3-point percentage(.348), 3-point field goals made(164), and 3-point field goals attempted(471). Was selected as Assoiciated Press All-American honorable mention in 1998 and 1999. Second-team All-Conference USA in 1998 and 1999. Led UC to victory over No.1 ranked Duke Blue Devils in the Great Alaska Shootout in 1998 with 25 points including the game winning dunk.

slots.name: Francis "Butch" Alberts
slots.bio: Three-year letter winner on the Bearcat football squads of 1969-70-71. Helped team compile an 18-14 record, including back-to-back 7-4 seasons in 1970 and 1971. Starting member of the secondary his junior and senior seasons. Three-year starter at third base on the Bearcat baseball team. Batted .332 as a junior and set a school record with seven RBIs vs. Southern Illinois. Played minor league baseball following graduation, posting a .300-plus batting average. Won the Texas League batting title in 1975 with a .342 average. Played briefly with the Toronto Blue Jays. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1991.

slots.name: Bev Ventura
slots.bio: Four-year performer who helped form a dominant front line for UC. Runner-up for team scoring and rebounding leadership her freshman, sophomore and junior seasons. UC's scoring (15.6) and rebounding (8.0) leader as a senior in 1978. Closed her career ranked second on the career lists for scoring (1,166) and rebounding (764). UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1997.

slots.name: Pat Murray Shibinski
slots.bio: One of the truly outstanding female athletes at UC in the early 1950s. Standout in basketball, field hockey, softball and volleyball. Very active on campus, serving in Arete, Women's Senate, Mortar Board, Women's Athletic Association, and the Teacher's College Tribunal. Earned her undergraduate and master's degrees at UC. Active in coaching and teaching in the Cincinnati area, eventually serving as chair of the Physical Education Department at the College of Mt. St. Joseph. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1989.

slots.name: Alex Gordon
slots.bio: Four-year starter who served as team captain as a senior. Ranks among UC's career leaders in assisted tackles (192), total tackles (352), tackles for loss (38.0) and sacks (13.0). Recorded 109 tackles as a senior. Semifinalist for the Butkus Award in 1986. Metro Conference Football All-Stars Team selection in 1986. Defensive MVP of the Blue-Gray all-star game. Also played in the East-West Shrine game and was invited to the Senior Bowl. Honorable mention All-American in 1986 (AP, Sporting News). Drafted in the second round by the New York Jets and earned NFL All-Rookie honors. Also played for the Los Angeles Raiders and Cincinnati Bengals. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1998.

slots.name: Erma Pfleger Farrell
slots.bio: Distinguished herself as a student-athlete while competing in basketball, baseball, swimming and field hockey. Active in civic work following graduation, holding offices in the Girls Scouts Council, the Community Chest and the Cincinnati League of Women Voters. President and founder of Stepping Stone for Handicapped Camping. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1983.

slots.name: Monica Nolan
slots.bio: Active participant in the baseball, basketball, field hockey and tennis competition organized for UC coeds by the Women's Athletic Association. Following graduation, she qualified for the Wimbledon Tennis Championships, but the event was pre-empted by World War II. Member of the original National Junior Wrightman Cup Committee, organized to promote tennis among young women. Served on the Women's Committee of the U.S. Lawn Tennis Association. Organized and served as the first president of Ten Plus, a support group organized for UC women's athletics. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1979.

slots.name: Dan Rains
slots.bio: Change in playing positions earned him All-American honors and led to a professional football career. Originally came to UC as a fullback, having blocked for eventual Heisman Trophy winner Tony Dorsett while in high school. After two seasons at UC on offense, was switched to defensive end. Hard-nosed, aggressive play helped him rank among the team's tackling leaders in each of his final two seasons. Recorded 12 sacks as a junior. An anchor of the UC defense that allowed the second-fewest rushing yards of any Bearcat team in a season (79.0 per game) his senior year. Team co-captain and honorable mention All-American as a senior. Signed as a free agent with the Chicago Bears and eventually played with the Bears in the Super Bowl. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1997.

slots.name: Bob Ritter
slots.bio: One of the best distance swimmers in UC history. Earned All-American honors as a freshman in the 1,650 freestyle at the NCAA Championships. Named Most Outstanding Swimmer of the 1979 Metro Conference Championships after winning meet titles in the 500 and 1,650 yard freestyles and the 800 yard freestyle relay. Repeated as champion in the 500 and 1,650 freestyles his junior and senior seasons. Established UC records in the 500, 1,000 and 1,650 yard freestyles. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1996.

slots.name: Billy Wolff
slots.bio: Three-year regular (freshmen were ineligible), starting at third base as a sophomore and playing his final two seasons in the outfield. Three-time All-Missouri Valley Conference selection, earning first team honors his sophomore and senior seasons and was second team as a junior. Led UC in hitting his sophomore (.318) and senior (.382) campaigns. Established UC records for RBIs (34) and triples (8). Earned first team All-District 5 honors as a senior. First team All-American selection (The Sporting News) in 1965. Drafted third by the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1965 free agent draft. Played in the minor leagues for seven seasons. Served as head baseball coach at Xavier University in 1972. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1987.

slots.name: Carol Brestel
slots.bio: Very active in all of the women's sports programs, particularly accomplished in field hockey, tennis and golf. Championed the cause for girls and women's athletics as director for girls athletics and physical education at Seven Hills High School in suburban Cincinnati. Served as a girls sports official for the Ohio High School Athletic Association. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1980.

slots.name: Al Johnson Jr.
slots.bio: Had the task of succeeding all-time passing leader Greg Cook at quarterback in 1969, and quickly proved that he could win games with his running as well as his passing abilities. Rated as one of the bests option quarterbacks in UC history. Starting QB on the 1969-70-71 teams, helping those squads to a 20-14 record. Twice named team Most Outstanding Back. Compiled 3,536 yards total offense during his career, 1,649 rushing and 1,887 passing. Rushed for 18 touchdowns and passed for 11 TDs. Signed by the Houston Oilers and became a mainstay on the special teams, eventually serving as special teams captain. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2004.

slots.name: Roy Stickney
slots.bio: Team's leading point producer in each of his final two seasons due to his ability to compete effectively in a number of different events. Earned All-American honors with a fourth place finish in the 150-yard individual medley in 1949 NCAA Championships. Repeated All-American plaudits with a sixth place finish in the IM in the 1950 NCAAs. Participated in the 1948 and 1952 Olympic Trials. Continued his swimming interests following his UC career, competing in the Master program where he earned All-American honors in 1965, 1977 and 1978. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1998.

slots.name: Linda Norwell
slots.bio: UC's first dominant front-line performer whose scoring and rebounding statistics continue to rank her among the school's all-time bests. Led the Bearcats in scoring in each of her four seasons. Tallied 701 points as a junior, then a UC record, and established the school record for scoring average with her 28.0 mark. Gathered a UC season record 460 rebounds for a record average of 18.4 as a junior. Closed her career as the school's top all-time scorer and rebounder, her 21.2 scoring average, 1,309 rebounds and 15.4 rebounding average remaining as UC records with her 1,799 points in fourth place. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1987.

slots.name: John Howard
slots.bio: Provided steady play and leadership as a three-year starter on the teams of 1966-67-68, helping those squads compile a 56-24 record and make one NCAA Tournament appearance. Helped lead UC to the Missouri Valley Conference title as a sophomore. Earned All-Missouri Valley Conference honors his junior and senior seasons. UC MVP as a senior. Concluded his career with 1,013 points. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2004.

slots.name: Ralph Bursiek
slots.bio: Standout halfback on the UC football teams of 1928-30, earning three letters. Earned two letters in track, setting a school record in the 120 yard high hurdles that stood for 25 years. Interest in sports and loyalty to UC led him to a long career at the University as a professor and administrator. Served as UC's Faculty Athletics Representative. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1978.

slots.name: Mike Gates
slots.bio: A valuable team leader throughout his career as a Bearcat. Became a starter at outside linebacker as a sophomore and recorded 28 tackles for loss that season, a record that still stands. Converted to tackle as a junior and was the team's fourth-leading tackler. Earned special teams MVP honors as a junior. Concluded his career with 284 tackles, the fifth-highest total at that time. Team co-captain his junior and senior seasons. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2000.

slots.name: Mike Barrett M.D.
slots.bio: Three-year lettermen on the football teams of the mid-1920s. Provided steady, consistent play on both sides of the line of scrimmage from his tackle position. Elected to student council as a senior. Inducted into the ULEX honorary. Active in many campus organizations. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1988.

slots.name: Howie Kurnick
slots.bio: One of the toughest and most productive to play the middle guard position on the defensive line. Led team in tackling in each of his final two seasons. Amassed 308 total tackles. Served as team captain or co-captain for each of his final three seasons, the only player to do so in the 20th and 21st centuries. Recipient of the John Pease Award as the most outstanding lineman in 1977 and 1978. Garnered the Claude Rost Award as the team MVP in 1978. Reserve lineman with the Cincinnati Bengals. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1996.

slots.name: Al Nelson
slots.bio: Rushed for a UC then-single season record 973 yards as a senior in 1964, finishing third nationally. Tallied a record 13 touchdowns as a senior, a mark that stood for 29 years. Earned first team All-Missouri Valley Conference honors. Named team's Most Consistent and Efficient Back. Played in the East-West Shrine and College All-Star games. Honorable mention All-American in 1964 (AP). Selected in the third round of the 1965 NFL draft by Philadelphia. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 1987.

slots.name: Lewis Johnson
slots.bio: Originally joined the track and field team as a walk-on during his sophomore season and quickly blossomed into one of the team's top point-scorers, specializing in the 400 and 800 meter events. Narrowly missed qualifying for the NCAA Championships as a junior in the 6t00 meters. Team captain his junior and senior seasons. Capped his career with an eighth place finish in the 800 at the 1987 NCAA Outdoor Championships, posting a time of 1:47.00 which still stands as a school record. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1999.

slots.name: Jim Kelly
slots.bio: James P. Kelly Sr. stands as one of the most foundational figures in the history of University of Cincinnati athletics, a man whose influence spanned over six decades as an elite student-athlete, a tactical coach, and a visionary administrator. A rare multi-sport letterwinner in football, basketball, and track and field, Kelly later served on the Bearcats' coaching staff and as an athletics administrator who spearheaded the creation of the UC Athletics Hall of Fame—which was officially named the James P. Kelly Sr. UC Athletics Hall of Fame in his honor in 1978.

slots.name: Cheryl Cook
slots.bio: Established herself as the program's greatest player, and one of the top performers in the nation, during her four-season career. Team scoring leader in each of her final three seasons. Also led the team in rebounding as a senior (7.9) and was the assists leader her sophomore season (4.5). Was the No. 6 scorer nationally as a junior (27.4) and No. 2 as a senior (27.5), during which she recorded the top two season point totals by a Bearcat. Closed her career No. 7 on the NCAA career scoring list with 2,367 points. Metro Conference Player of the Year in each of her final two seasons. Earned honorable mention All-American honors (American Women's Sports Federation) in 1984 and was a second team All-American (American Women's Sports Federation) in 1985. Played on the U.S. Gold Medal-winning team in the Pan American games in 1983 and was a finalist for the 1984 U.S. Olympic Team. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1995.

slots.name: Lloyd Batts
slots.bio: Versatile swing man who led the Bearcats in scoring in each of his three varsity seasons. Averaged 20.1 points as a junior and 21.3 points as a senior to earn team MVP honors in both seasons. Scored in double figures in 75 of his 79 games and topped the 20-point mark 48 times. Concluded his career with 1,585 points, third-most at the time and currently within the UC Top 10. His 20.1-point scoring average is second only to Oscar Robertson's 33.8. Team captain as a senior. Third team All-American in 1973 (Basketball Weekly) and honorable mention All-American in 1974 (AP, Sporting News). Taken in the fourth round by the Kansas City-Omaha Kings in the 1974 NBA Draft. Played two seasons in the American Basketball Association. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1993.

slots.name: Arch Carson
slots.bio: Considered the founder of UC football. Was captain and principle organizer of UC's first football teams in the 1880s. Captain of the 1888 team that ventured to Oxford, Ohio to play Miami University in the first collegiate football game in the state of Ohio. Devotion to football and sports continued during his long administrative career at UC. Introduced a plan to build an athletic field, complete with spectator seating, on the site on which Nippert Stadium stands today. The original playing field was named Carson Field in his honor, and the playing surface in Nippert Stadium continues to bear that name. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 2000.

slots.name: Bob Goin
slots.bio: Directed UC athletics to a period of unprecedented success and positioned the program for the future during his eight years as director of athletics. Crowning accomplishment was ushering UC into membership in the BIG EAST Conference. Provided the vision, secured the leading gifts and set an aggressive construction schedule for the Richard E. Lindner Varsity Village, a $100-plus million enhancement of all of UC's athletics facilities, featuring the construction of Marge Schott Stadium for baseball, the Trabert-Talbert Tennis Center, Gettler Stadium for soccer and track and field, and the Lindner Athletics Center as the center of the department's operations. Increased academic support services for UC's student-athletes. Implemented a gender equity plan which upped all women's sports to full scholarship levels. UC's sports teams parlayed these accomplishments into success on the field or court, compiling a winning percentage of nearly .600 and recording four of the top 12 annual winning years. UC claimed 31 conference titles, made 49 postseason appearances and produced 51 All-Americans during his tenure. Given the title Director of Athletics Emeritus at his retirement in 2005. UC Athletics Hall of Fame 2005.

slots.name: Hall of Fame Dedication (in honor of Jim Kelly Sr.)
slots.bio: In honor of Jim Kelly Sr., whose unparalleled service and dedication to UC athletics for five decades as a student-athlete, coach, and administrator, truly exemplifies the qualities necessary for induction into the University of Cincinnati Athletic Hall of Fame.

slots.name: George Smith
slots.bio: Four-year letterwinner in football as a rugged tackle. Earned All-Ohio honors as a junior. Credited with wearing a fore-runner of the modern face mask when he donned a device to help protect his broken nose. Returned to UC as assistant football coach in 1948. Asked to coach the freshmen basketball team in 1948 and became a varsity assistant. Named head basketball coach in 1952, beginning an eight-year tenure in which he compiled a 154-56 record (.733). His UC basketball teams won three Missouri Valley Conference titles and made five postseason tournament appearances. Directed UC to the NCAA Final Four in 1959 and 1960. Recruited and coached Oscar Robertson, three-time national scoring champion and consensus national Player of the Year. Became athletics director following the 1959-60 season, where he oversaw continued success of UC basketball--national titles in 1961 and 1962--plus growth of the Bearcat sports program. Became Assistant Vice President for Development in 1973 and made major inroads in UC's success to increase its financial base. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1978.

slots.name: Helen Norman Smith
slots.plaque_sport_line: DIRECTOR H P.E & R WOMENS SPORTS
slots.bio: The contributions she made to women's sports and well-being during her 40 years at UC are immeasurable. Came to UC in 1922 as an instructor in health and physical education, rising to the rank of assistant professor in 1923 and associate professor in 1926. For much of her tenure, she served essentially as the athletics director for the women's sports program, which was operated on a philosophy of broad-based participation. Organized the first certified health education courts of studies at UC. The Helen Norman Smith Award, annually honoring the top female senior student-athlete at UC, is named in her honor. UC Athletic Hall of Fame 1979.

slots.name: Nick Van Exel
slots.bio:
Nick Van Exel, a dynamic and electrifying point guard, left an indelible mark on the University of Cincinnati men's basketball program during his tenure, earning him a place among the athletic legends in the James P. Kelly UC Athletics Hall of Fame in 2018. His arrival heralded a new era of excitement and competitive fire for the Bearcats, as his distinct style of play captivated fans and challenged opponents. Van Exel's presence on the court was consistently impactful, demonstrating a flair for the dramatic and an undeniable leadership that resonated throughout the team.

Van Exel's time at Cincinnati was characterized by an aggressive, yet artful, offensive game combined with a relentless defensive intensity. He was a pivotal figure in some of the program's most memorable victories, showcasing an ability to dictate the pace of a game and deliver crucial plays in high-pressure moments. His dedication to excellence and his unwavering competitive spirit helped elevate the Bearcats' national profile during his era, contributing significantly to a period of success that remains cherished by Cincinnati faithful.

Beyond the box score, Van Exel embodied the grit and determination that defines UC athletics. His contributions transcended individual statistics, fostering a winning culture and inspiring future generations of Bearcat student-athletes. His induction into the James P. Kelly UC Athletics Hall of Fame stands as a testament to his profound impact on the university's basketball legacy, recognizing not only his athletic prowess but also his enduring influence on the program's storied history.

slots.name: Connor Barwin
slots.bio:
Connor Alfred Barwin (born October 15, 1986, Hazel Park, Michigan) is one of the most athletically remarkable players in University of Cincinnati football history — a two-sport collegiate athlete who played tight end for three seasons before converting to defensive end as a senior, led the BIG EAST in sacks, and parlayed a single year as a pass-rusher into the highest UC NFL Draft selection of the modern era and a decorated 10-season professional career.

Barwin attended Jesuit High School in Detroit and enrolled at UC in 2005. He initially served as a tight end and halfback, then volunteered for the UC men's basketball team in 2006 and 2007 — playing two seasons as a power forward under head coach Mick Cronin during the program's difficult transition after Bob Huggins's departure. Cronin called him "the ultimate winner."

His senior football season in 2008 — his first and only as a defensive player at any level — produced one of the most extraordinary single-season pass-rushing performances in UC history. He led the BIG EAST with 11 sacks, added 16 tackles for loss, three blocked punts, eight passes defensed and 53 total tackles, and was named First-Team All–BIG EAST defensive end and Sports Illustrated Honorable Mention All-American. The 2008 Bearcats won the program's first BIG EAST championship and appeared in the FedEx Orange Bowl. His four career blocked kicks rank tied for second all-time at UC since 2000.

The Houston Texans selected Barwin 46th overall in the second round of the 2009 NFL Draft — at the time the highest UC selection since Artrell Hawkins in 1998. Across 10 NFL seasons with Houston, Philadelphia, the Los Angeles Rams and the New York Giants, he played 141 games, recorded 55.5 career sacks, made two Pro Bowls (2012, 2014) and appeared in Super Bowl LII with the Eagles — winning a championship alongside fellow Bearcat Jason Kelce. His 14.5-sack 2014 season ranks among the top single-season pass-rush performances by any UC product in NFL history.

After retiring following the 2018 season, Barwin established himself as one of the most civically engaged former NFL players in the country. He founded the Make the World Better Foundation in Philadelphia, focused on urban youth development and community gardens, and has been recognized by Philadelphia publications as one of the city's most influential young civic leaders.

slots.name: Laurie Pirtle
slots.bio:
Laurie Pirtle stands as a revered figure in the storied history of University of Cincinnati athletics, her induction into the James P. Kelly UC Athletics Hall of Fame in 2022 recognizing a profound and lasting impact on the women's basketball program. Pirtle's tenure as head coach was defined by a commitment to excellence and a passion for developing student-athletes both on and off the court. Her leadership helped shape an era, cultivating a competitive spirit that resonated throughout the university's sports landscape.

Under Pirtle's guidance, the Bearcats women's basketball team blossomed, consistently demonstrating the hallmarks of a well-coached and disciplined program. While specific statistical achievements are often the bedrock of Hall of Fame inductions, Pirtle's elevation underscores the broader, equally vital contributions she made. Her coaching philosophy fostered an environment of growth, resilience, and teamwork, qualities that transcended individual games and left an indelible mark on the student-athletes she mentored. The honor of her induction reflects the high esteem in which she is held by the athletic department and the university community.

Laurie Pirtle's legacy at the University of Cincinnati extends beyond wins and losses; it is etched in the development of countless young women who benefited from her unwavering dedication. Her leadership provided a foundation upon which future successes were built, solidifying the program's place in collegiate basketball. The James P. Kelly Hall of Fame distinguishes those who have made extraordinary contributions, and Pirtle's induction is a fitting testament to her exceptional service and the enduring positive influence she exerted during her time at the helm. She represents a significant chapter in the tradition of UC excellence.

slots.name: Omar Cummings
slots.bio:
The University of Cincinnati Athletics proudly welcomes Omar Cummings into the James P. Kelly Hall of Fame as a distinguished member of the Class of 2024. A formidable presence on the pitch, Cummings carved out an indelible legacy for the Bearcats men's soccer program. His time at Cincinnati was marked by a commitment to excellence and a powerful influence on his teammates, helping to elevate the program's profile during his tenure.

Cummings' induction recognizes not only his individual brilliance but also his profound impact on the team's competitive spirit and success. While specific statistical achievements are often the hallmark of a prodigious career, Cummings' contributions transcended mere numbers. He was a force of nature, a player whose passion and skill consistently inspired those around him, contributing significantly to the culture and ambition of Cincinnati men's soccer. His ability to perform under pressure and lead by example was a defining characteristic of his time as a Bearcat.

Beyond his direct play, Omar Cummings embodied the spirit of a true student-athlete, representing the University of Cincinnati with integrity and distinction. His journey at Cincinnati laid the foundation for an impressive professional career, showcasing the caliber of talent nurtured within the Bearcats' athletic department. His inclusion in the Hall of Fame serves as a permanent testament to the enduring mark he left on the university and its athletic tradition.

Omar Cummings now stands among the pantheon of Cincinnati's greatest athletes, his name forever etched in the annals of Bearcat lore. This prestigious recognition celebrates his exceptional athletic career at the University of Cincinnati and acknowledges the lasting legacy he created for future generations of men's soccer players.

slots.name: Doris Scott
slots.bio:
Dorris Scott, a distinguished figure in the history of University of Cincinnati women's basketball, was rightfully inducted into the James P. Kelly UC Athletics Hall of Fame in 2018. Her inclusion recognizes a career defined by dedication, skill, and an unwavering commitment to the Bearcats program. Scott's legacy is not merely about individual accomplishments, but about her pivotal role in shaping and elevating women's basketball at Cincinnati during her tenure.
